'''Ebbor Gorge''' is a [[limestone]] [[Canyon|gorge]] in [[Somerset]], England, designated and notified in 1952 as a {{convert|63.5|ha|acre|adj=on}} [[biological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in the [[Mendip Hills]]. It was donated to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1967 and is now managed by [[Natural England]] as a [[national nature reserves in England|national nature reserve]].

The gorge was cut mostly into the [[Clifton Down Limestone]], part of the Lower [[Carboniferous]] [[Pembroke Limestone Group|Pembroke Group]], by water. The site was occupied by humans in the [[Neolithic]] Era and their tools and flint arrow heads have been discovered, along with pottery from the [[Bronze Age]]. There are also fossils of small mammals from the Late [[Last glacial period|Devensian]]. The nature reserve provides a habitat for a variety of flora and fauna, including flowers, butterflies and bats.

==Geology==

Ebbor Gorge lies on the southwest-facing slope of the Mendip Hills and consists of a steep-sided ravine cut into 350-million-year-old [[Carboniferous Limestone]] of the [[Dinantian]]. The gorge was cut into [[Clifton Down Limestone]] by meltwater in the [[Pleistocene]] [[epoch (geology)|Epoch]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Wookey Hole and Ebbor Gorge|url=http://www.bgs.ac.uk/mendips/localities/wookey.html|publisher=British Geological Survey|access-date=22 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Donovan|first=D.T.|title=The late pleistocene sequence at Wells, Somerset|journal=Proceedings of the University of Bristol Speleological Society|year=1988|volume=18|issue=2|pages=241–257|url=http://www.ubss.org.uk/resources/proceedings/vol18/UBSS_Proc_18_2_241-257.pdf|format=PDF}}</ref> The lowest part of the gorge is formed in the Namurian Quartzitic Sandstone Group and the South Wales Lower Coal Measures, over which younger limestones have been thrust to the north-east, as demonstrated by the BGS maps (1:50,000 sheet 280, Wells).  An example of the rare mineral [[mendipite]] was found at the head of the gorge.<ref>{{cite book|last=Toulson|first=Shirley|title=The Mendip Hills: A Threatened Landscape|year=1984|publisher=Victor Gollanz Ltd|isbn=978-0-575-03453-2|page=32}}</ref>

A stream issuing to the west of the site runs down the tributary valley of Hope Wood before joining the main gorge. The original watercourse which may have cut the gorge into the limestone became diverted underground and now emerges at [[Wookey Hole Caves]] to form the [[River Axe (Bristol Channel)|River Axe]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Smith|first=David Ingle|title=Limestone and Caves of the Mendip Hills|year=1975|publisher=David & Charles|isbn=978-0-7153-6572-4|page=120}}</ref>

==History==

Various caves within the gorge were inhabited by [[neolithic]] people from which flint tools are held in the [[Wells and Mendip Museum]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Lewis|first=Jodie |author-link=Jodie Lewis |title=The Everton flint collection in Wells Museum|journal=Proceedings of the University of Bristol Speleological Society|year=1998|volume=21|issue=2|pages=141–148|url=http://www.ubss.org.uk/resources/proceedings/vol21/UBSS_Proc_21_2_141-148.pdf|format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Brown|first=Graham|title=Dispersed settlements on the southern Mendip escarpment. The earthwork evidence|url=http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/72_2008WEB.pdf|format=PDF|work=Research Department Report Series no 72-2008|publisher=English Heritage|access-date=22 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224105017/http://services.english-heritage.org.uk/ResearchReportsPdfs/72_2008WEB.pdf|archive-date=24 December 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=nateng>{{cite web|title=Ebbor Gorge NNR|url=http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designations/nnr/1006052.aspx|publisher=Natural England|access-date=19 May 2014}}</ref> One particularly fine flint flake can be seen in the museum at [[King John's Hunting Lodge, Axbridge|King John's Hunting Lodge]] in [[Axbridge]].<ref>{{cite journal|last=Bond|first=Clive Jonathon|title=The later upper palaeolithic open sites and settlement trajectories. The evidence from the Mendip Hills, south-west Britain|url=http://www.naturalsciences.be/mars/groups/fnrs-contact-group/notae-praehistoricae/resolveUid/9d61bc5a9a1b9ac0c05fc0fc4ee55b69|journal=Notae Praehistoricae|year=2013|volume=33|pages=179–192}}{{Dead link|date=February 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Human and animal bones from the [[Neolithic]] were recovered from Outlook Cave in 1907.<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Outlook Cave|num=1010711|access-date=15 February 2015}}</ref> Bones from the [[Palaeolithic]] have been found at Savory's Hole.<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Savory's Hole|num=1012061|access-date=22 February 2015}}</ref>

Several caves occur within the Gorge, of which Bridged Pot and Gully Cave provide some of the best Late [[Last glacial period|Devensian]] small-mammal assemblages known from Britain. Most of the deposits remain in situ and include [[Pika|steppe pika]], [[Arctic lemming]], [[Norway lemming]], various [[vole]]s, [[red deer]] and [[reindeer]].<ref name=engnature>{{cite web | title=Ebbor Gorge | work=English Nature | url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1004346.pdf|format=PDF | access-date=22 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Papworth|first=Martin|title=Deep Time in Ebbor Gorge|url=http://archaeologynationaltrustsw.wordpress.com/2013/08/11/deep-time-in-ebbor-gorge/|work=Archeology|publisher=National Trust|access-date=22 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Wolves and wildcats: surviving the end of the last ice age in Somerset|url=http://www.hhgs.org.uk/monthly_meetings/previous_meetings/wolves_and_wildcats/wolves_and_wildcats.htm|publisher=Harrow and Hillingdon Geological Society|access-date=19 May 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Learning & Leading Fieldwork Apprentices|url=http://www.rgs.org/NR/rdonlyres/A3B13E99-7E2D-4D70-94A5-9FEAE564DBA9/0/FieldworkApprenticeshipProfile_2010_LisaHowell.pdf|format=PDF|publisher=Royal Geographical Society|access-date=19 May 2014}}</ref> [[Bronze Age]] finds include pottery from the [[Beaker culture]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Bridged Pot Shelter, Ebbor Gorge, Wookey, Somerset|url=http://capra.group.shef.ac.uk/1/swest.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204160157/http://capra.group.shef.ac.uk/1/swest.html|archive-date=4 February 2012|work=A Gazetteer of English Caves, Fissures and Rock Shelters Containing Human Remains|publisher=University of Sheffield|access-date=22 December 2013}}</ref> a stone axe and flint knife.<ref>{{cite web|title=Bridged Pot Hole, Ebbor Gorge|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/24332|website=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=4 October 2014}}</ref>

==Current use==
[[File:Ebborgrogeplaque.jpg|thumb|left|Plaque at Ebbor Gorge commemorating the donation of the land]]
A {{convert|40|ha|acre|adj=on}} area of the gorge is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]], and managed by [[Natural England]] as a [[national nature reserves in England|national nature reserve]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designatedareas/nnr/1006052.aspx |archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20140605090108/http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designatedareas/nnr/1006052.aspx|archive-date=5 June 2014 |title=Ebbor Gorge NNR |access-date=31 January 2010 |work=Natural England }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Things to see and do|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/mendip-hills/things-to-see-and-do/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=21 December 2013}}</ref> The land was donated to the National Trust by Mrs G.W. Hodgkinson, in 1967, in memory of [[Winston Churchill]].<ref name="curio">{{cite book |title=Curiosities of Somerset |last=Leete-Hodge |first=Lornie |year=1985 |publisher=Bossiney Books |location=Bodmin |isbn=0-906456-98-3 |page=24 }}</ref> The site was purchased in 1931 by [[Wookey Hole Caves|Wookey Hole Caves Ltd]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Beauty Spot Known to Few Bristolians|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000264/19310717/023/0004|access-date=4 October 2014|work=Western Daily Press|date=17 July 1931|page=4| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The site is close to [[Wookey Hole|Wookey Hole village]] and [[Wookey Hole Caves|caves]] and offers views across the [[Somerset Levels]] to [[Glastonbury Tor]] and beyond. There are three marked trails of varying lengths around the steeply wooded gorge, the longest being {{convert|3|km}} long,<ref name=nateng/> the shortest of which is suitable for wheelchair users.<ref>{{cite book|last=Toulson|first=Shirley|title=The Mendip Hills: A Threatened Landscape|year=1984|publisher=Victor Gollanz Ltd|isbn=978-0-575-03453-2|pages=128–129}}</ref>

==Biology and ecology==
[[File:Ebbor Gorge 2.jpg|thumb|The path into the gorge]]

Because of the ecology of the area {{convert|63.5|ha|acre}} was designated as a [[biological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in 1952.<ref name=engnature/> The ground [[flora]] is indicative of the calcareous nature of the site, with [[Mercurialis perennis|dog's mercury]] (''Mercurialis perennis'') being locally dominant. Many of the associated species are characteristic of [[ancient woodland]]. [[Anemone nemorosa|Wood anemone]] (''Anemone nemorosa'') and [[Hyacinthoides non-scripta|common bluebell]] (''Hyacinthoides non-scripta'') are both locally abundant. The valley of the main gorge is humid and provides ideal conditions for [[Fungus|fungi]] and [[fern]]s. It contains a substantial assemblage of [[bryophyte]]s with over 120 species recorded including the nationally rare ''[[Bryum canariense]]'' and the very rare ''[[Amblystegiella confervoides]]''.<ref name=engnature/>

The varied age and canopy structure of woodland encourages a high diversity of [[Butterfly|butterflies]], nationally scarce species including the [[white-letter hairstreak]] (''Strymonidia walbum'') and [[high brown fritillary]] (''Fabriciana adippe''), while species such as the [[chalkhill blue]] (''Lysandra coridon'') and [[brown argus]] (''Aricia agestis'') occur on the limestone grassland.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ebbor Gorge|url=http://www.ukbms.org/SiteFactsheet.aspx?siteId=23|publisher=United Kingdom Butterfly Monitoring Scheme|access-date=19 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140519223906/http://www.ukbms.org/SiteFactsheet.aspx?siteId=23|archive-date=19 May 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> [[Greater horseshoe bat]]s (''Rhinolophus ferrumequinum'') and [[lesser horseshoe bat|lesser horseshoes]] (''Rhinolophus hipposideros'') regularly use sites in the Gorge as [[Hibernaculum (zoology)|hibernacular]] roosts.<ref name=engnature/> The site also supports [[Bird of prey|birds of prey]] and a few red deer.<ref>{{cite book|last=Toulson|first=Shirley|title=The Mendip Hills: A Threatened Landscape|year=1984|publisher=Victor Gollanz Ltd|isbn=978-0-575-03453-2|page=128}}</ref>

3233991.title: Dunster Castle
3233991.extract:
Dunster Castle is a former motte and bailey castle, now a country house, in the village of Dunster, Somerset, England. The castle lies on the top of a steep hill called the Tor, and has been fortified since the late Anglo-Saxon period. After the Norman Conquest of England in the 11th century, William de Mohun constructed a timber castle on the site as part of the pacification of Somerset. A stone shell keep was built on the motte by the start of the 12th century, and the castle survived a siege during the early years of the Anarchy. At the end of the 14th century the de Mohuns sold the castle to the Luttrell family, who continued to occupy the property until the late 20th century.
The castle was expanded several times by the Luttrell family during the 17th and 18th centuries; they built a large manor house within the Lower Ward of the castle in 1617, and this was extensively modernised, first during the 1680s and then during the 1760s. The medieval castle walls were mostly destroyed following the siege of Dunster Castle at the end of the First English Civil War, when Parliament ordered the defences to be slighted to prevent their further use. In the 1860s and 1870s, the architect Anthony Salvin was employed to remodel the castle to fit Victorian tastes; this work extensively changed the appearance of Dunster to make it appear more Gothic and Picturesque.
Following the death of Alexander Luttrell in 1944, the family was unable to afford the death duties on his estate. The castle and surrounding lands were sold off to a property firm, the family continuing to live in the castle as tenants. The Luttrells bought back the castle in 1954, but in 1976 Colonel Sir Walter Luttrell gave Dunster Castle and most of its contents to the National Trust, which operates it as a tourist attraction. It is a Grade I listed building and scheduled monument.

'''Dunster Castle''' is a former [[motte and bailey]] castle, now a [[English country house|country house]], in the village of [[Dunster]], [[Somerset]], England. The castle lies on the top of a steep hill called the Tor, and has been fortified since the late [[Anglo-Saxon]] period. After the [[Norman Conquest]] of England in the 11th century, [[William de Mohun]] constructed a timber castle on the site as part of the pacification of Somerset. A stone [[shell keep]] was built on the motte by the start of the 12th century, and the castle survived a siege during the early years of [[the Anarchy]]. At the end of the 14th century the de Mohuns sold the castle to the [[Earl of Carhampton|Luttrell family]], who continued to occupy the property until the late 20th century.

The castle was expanded several times by the Luttrell family during the 17th and 18th centuries; they built a large [[manor house]] within the Lower Ward of the castle in 1617, and this was extensively modernised, first during the 1680s and then during the 1760s. The medieval castle walls were mostly destroyed following the siege of Dunster Castle at the end of the [[First English Civil War]], when [[Parliament of England|Parliament]] ordered the defences to be [[slighting|slighted]] to prevent their further use. In the 1860s and 1870s, the architect [[Anthony Salvin]] was employed to remodel the castle to fit Victorian tastes; this work extensively changed the appearance of Dunster to make it appear more [[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] and [[Picturesque]].

Following the death of Alexander Luttrell in 1944, the family was unable to afford the [[inheritance tax|death duties]] on his estate. The castle and surrounding lands were sold off to a property firm, the family continuing to live in the castle as tenants. The Luttrells bought back the castle in 1954, but in 1976 Colonel Sir [[Walter Luttrell]] gave Dunster Castle and most of its contents to the [[National Trust]], which operates it as a [[tourist attraction]]. It is a Grade I [[listed building]] and [[scheduled monument]].

==History==

===11th to 12th centuries===
{{Further|topic=the medieval barony of Dunster|Feudal barony of Dunster}}
Dunster Castle was positioned on a steep, {{convert|200|ft|m|-1|adj=mid|-high}} hill, sometimes called the Tor, overlooking the village of [[Dunster]] in [[Somerset]].<ref>Mackenzie, p.54.</ref>{{#tag:ref|Geologically, the hill is an outcrop of Hangman Grits, a type of red [[sandstone]].<ref>''[http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/catalogue/adsdata/arch-954-1/dissemination/pdf/michaelh1-61588_1.pdf Dunster Castle Roof Repairs 2006–2008]'', (PDF) p.1, Michael Heaton Heritage Consultants, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref>|group="nb"}} During the early medieval period the sea reached the base of the hill, close to the mouth of the [[River Avill]], offering a natural defence and making the village an inland port.<ref>Dunning, pp.37–39; Creighton, pp.41–42.</ref> Several [[Iron Age]] [[hillfort]]s were built close to Dunster, including [[Bat's Castle]], [[Black Ball Camp]] and Grabbist Hill, but the earliest evidence of a fortification at Dunster was an [[Anglo-Saxon]] ''[[burgh]]''.<ref>''[http://ads.ahds.ac.uk/catalogue/search/fr.cfm?rcn=NMR_NATINV-36857 Black Ball Camp]'', Arts and Humanities Data Service, accessed 28 September 2007; ''[http://ads.ahds.ac.uk/catalogue/search/fr.cfm?rcn=NMR_NATINV-36851 univallate Hillfort]'', Arts and Humanities Data Service, accessed 28 September 2007; Gathercole, Clare, ''[http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/EUS_DunsterText.pdf An archaeological assessment of Dunster]'' (PDF), Somerset County Council, accessed 1 October 2011</ref> This was built on the summit of the hill and was possibly intended to protect the region against sea-borne raiders; by the mid-11th century it was controlled by a local nobleman called Aelfric.<ref>Mackenzie, p.54; Garnett, p.38.</ref>

[[File:Dunster Castle map.png|thumb|left|Map of Dunster Castle and immediate area: A — Motte; B — [[Dunster Working Watermill|Watermill]]; C — Castle; D — Great Gatehouse; E [[River Avill]]]]
In 1066 the [[Norman invasion of England|Normans invaded south-east England]], defeating the English forces at the [[Battle of Hastings]]: in the aftermath of the victory, [[William the Conqueror]] entrusted the conquest of the south-west of England to his half-brother [[Robert of Mortain]].<ref>Prior, pp.74–75.</ref> Expecting stiff resistance, Robert marched west into Somerset, supported by forces under [[Walter of Douai]], who entered from the north; a third force, under the command of [[William de Moyon|William de Mohun]], landed by sea along the Somerset coast.<ref>Prior, p.75.</ref> William had been granted 68 manors in the region and by 1086 had established a castle at Dunster; this would form both the ''caput'', or principal castle, for his new lands, and help guard the coast against the threat of any fresh sea-borne attack, as well as controlling the coastal road running from Somerset to [[Gloucestershire]].<ref>Prior, p.76; Garnett, p.38.</ref> This first castle was a [[motte and bailey]] design, built upon the former Anglo-Saxon ''burgh''; the top of the Tor was [[Counterscarp|scarped]] to form the motte, or Upper Ward, and an area below shaped to form the bailey, or Lower Ward.<ref>Prior, p.108.</ref>{{#tag:ref|William de Mohun also built nearby [[Montacute Castle]] in Somerset.<ref>Lyte (1880), p.59.</ref>|group="nb"}}

Somerset became more stable in the aftermath of the post-invasion period and the unsuccessful 1068 rebellion against Norman rule. It was common in the period for the Normans to build religious houses to accompany major castles, and accordingly William de Mohun endowed a [[Benedictine]] [[priory]] at Dunster in 1090, along with its [[Bath Abbey|parent abbey at Bath]].<ref>Creighton, p.187; Lyte (1880), p.60.</ref> The River Avill was important for trade; the region around Dunster was rich with [[fishery|fisheries]] and [[vineyard]]s, and Dunster Castle prospered. Stone fortifications were built on the site during the early 12th century, probably forming a [[shell keep]] around the top of the motte.<ref>Prior, pp.108–109; Mackenzie, p.58; Lyte (1880), p.60; Garnett, p.5.</ref>

In the late 1130s England began to descend into a period of civil war known as [[the Anarchy]], during which the supporters of King [[Stephen of England|Stephen]] fought with those of the [[Empress Matilda]] for control of the kingdom. William de Mohun's eldest son, also called [[William de Mohun of Dunster, 1st Earl of Somerset|William]], was a noted supporter of Matilda, and Dunster was considered one of her faction's strongest castles in the south-west.<ref>Lyte (1880), p.61.</ref> In 1138 forces loyal to Stephen besieged the castle; a [[siege castle]] was built nearby, but all trace of it has been lost.<ref>Creighton, p.56; Mackenzie, p.58.</ref> William successfully held the castle and was made the [[Earl of Somerset]] by the grateful Empress. [[Chronicler]]s complained of the way in which he subsequently raided and controlled the region by force during the war, causing much destruction.<ref>Lyte (1880), p.61; Garnett, p.38.</ref> In the aftermath of the conflict, William's son, another William, inherited the castle after a short period of royal ownership under [[Henry II of England|Henry II]].<ref>Lyte (1880), p.62.</ref> William appears to have insisted that his tenants agree to help repair and maintain the castle walls as part of their [[feudal]] service.<ref>Lyte (1909), p.350.</ref>

===13th to 17th centuries===
[[File:The gatehouse, Dunster Castle - geograph.org.uk - 1215242.jpg|thumb|The 14th-century [[gatehouse|Great Gatehouse]]; when first built, the Lower Ward on the right would have been at the same height as the gateway]]
In the 13th century the Lower Ward was rebuilt in stone by Reynold Mohun; this was paid for in part by Reynold commuting his tenants' ongoing duty to repair the castle walls into a single, one-off financial payment to their lord, and partially through his marriage to a rich local heiress.<ref>Lyte (1909), pp.349–352.</ref> A survey of the castle in 1266 described the Upper Ward on the top of the motte as containing a hall with a buttery, a pantry, a kitchen, a bakehouse, the chapel of [[Saint Stephen]] and a knight's hall, guarded by three towers.<ref>Garnett, p.30; Lyte (1909), p.353.</ref> The Lower Ward included a [[granary]], two towers and a gatehouse; one of the towers, called the Fleming Tower, was used as a prison.<ref name=LyteP353>Lyte (1909), p.353.</ref> The castle stables lay outside the defences, further down the slope.<ref name=LyteP353/> By the end of the 13th century some of the castle's roofing had been covered in lead, while other parts still used wooden shingles.<ref name=DunningPP37>Dunning, pp.37–39.</ref>

In 1330 Sir [[John de Mohun, 2nd Baron Mohun|John de Mohun]] inherited the castle; John, although a notable knight, was childless and fell into considerable debt.<ref>Garnett, pp.38–39.</ref> His wife Joan took over the running of their estates, and when John died in 1376 she agreed to sell the castle to Lady Elizabeth Luttrell, the leading member of another major Norman family, for 5,000 [[Mark (money)|mark]]s, with the castle to transfer to Elizabeth on Joan's death.<ref name=GarnettP39>Garnett, p.39.</ref>{{#tag:ref|It is impossible to accurately compare 14th-century and modern prices or incomes. For comparison, 5,000 marks equated to £3,333 in 14th century pounds and represented over three times the typical average annual income for an early 15th-century baron.<ref>Pounds, p.148.</ref>|group="nb"}}{{#tag:ref|Historian Oliver Garnett notes that this sale of property from one woman to another was extremely unusual for the period.<ref name=GarnettP39/>|group="nb"}} At some point during this period additional stone buildings were constructed along the Lower Ward, on the side of the current mansion, and records suggest that a ditch, or [[moat]], may have existed around the base of the Tor in the 14th century.<ref>Lyte (1909), pp.354, 362.</ref>

Joan outlived Elizabeth, and in the event [[Sir Hugh Luttrell]], who was [[Henry V of England|Henry V's]] [[seneschal]] in [[Normandy]], finally took over the castle on Joan's death in 1404. The castle had suffered from a lack of investment during the final years of the Mohan's ownership, and Luttrell repaired and extended the castle at a cost of £252, constructing the Great Gatehouse and a [[barbican]] between 1419 and 1424.<ref>Dunning, pp.37–39; Emery, p.677; Garnet p.39.</ref>{{#tag:ref|It is impossible to accurately compare 14th-century and modern prices or incomes. For comparison, £252 is around a tenth of the cost of rebuilding the greater part of [[Hadleigh Castle]] in the 1360s.<ref>Alexander and Westlake, p.14.</ref>|group="nb"}} The new entrance lay at right-angles to the old and was three storeys high, built of imported Bristol red [[sandstone]], and contained extensive apartments; it formed a grand, if ill-defended, ceremonial route into the castle.<ref>Emery, pp.677–678; Garnett, p.30.</ref> The castle was reroofed with [[Cornwall|Cornish]] stone tiles.<ref>Garnett, p.30.</ref> By the 15th century the sea had receded, and the Luttrells created a [[Medieval deer park|deer park]] for the castle at Marshwood.<ref>''[http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/33568 Dunster New Park, Dunster]'', Somerset Historic Environment Record, [[Somerset County Council]], accessed 9 July 2011; Garnett, p.29.</ref> Such a park would have been highly prestigious and allowed the Luttrells to engage in [[hunting]], providing the castle with a supply of [[venison]] as well as generating income.<ref>Creighton, pp.190–191; Creighton and Higham, p.57.</ref>

[[File:Plan of Dunster Castle, pre-1860s.png|thumb|left|300px|Plan of the 17th-century mansion, including 18th-century additions: A – Parlour; B – Hall; C – Little Parlour; D – Steward's Room; E – Chapel; F – Kitchen; G – Service wing]]
During the 15th century, England was divided by the prolonged period of civil war now called the [[Wars of the Roses]]: the Luttrells were supporters of the [[House of Lancaster]]. In 1461, Sir James Luttrell died following the Lancastrian defeat at the [[Second Battle of St Albans]], and his family were deprived of their estates by the [[Yorkist]] [[Edward IV]].<ref name=GarnettP39/> The castle was given to the Herberts, but the Luttrells regained it on the accession of the Lancastrian [[Henry VII of England|Henry VII]] in 1485, when Dunster was restored to James' son, Sir Hugh Luttrell.<ref name=DunningPP37/> Hugh repaired the castle chapel and in the early 16th century his son, Sir Andrew Luttrell, built a new wall on the east side of the castle.<ref>Lyte (1909), p.364.</ref> Andrew's son Sir [[John Luttrell (soldier)|John Luttrell]], who inherited the castle, was a famous soldier, [[diplomat]], and [[courtier]] under [[Henry VIII]] and [[Edward VI]], serving in France and in Scotland during the conflicts of the [[Rough Wooing]].<ref>Phillips, pp.197, 207; Garnett, p.39.</ref> In 1542, the [[antiquarian]] [[John Leland (antiquarian)|John Leland]] reported the castle keep and buildings to be considerable disrepair, with the exception of the chapel, and after Sir John's death the castle was leased out for several years, first by his daughter, Mary, and then under his brother, Thomas.<ref>Garnett, pp.30, 39; ''[http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1558-1603/member/luttrell-thomas-1571 LUTTRELL, Thomas (d.1571), of Marshwood and Dunster Castle, Som]'', The History of Parliament Trust, accessed 28 May 2013.</ref>

By the time [[George Luttrell]] inherited the castle in 1571, it was dilapidated, with the family preferring to live in their house, now known as [[Court House, East Quantoxhead|Court House]], at [[East Quantoxhead]].<ref>Garnett, pp.30, 39.</ref> In 1617 George employed the architect [[William Arnold (architect)|William Arnold]], to create a new house in the Lower Ward of the castle. Arnold was an important architect in the south-west of England, and had managed the building of nearby [[Montacute House|Montacute]], [[Cranborne Manor|Cranborne House]] and also [[Wadham College, Oxford]].<ref name=GarnettP31>Garnett, p.31.</ref> The redesign expanded on some of the existing buildings and walls to create a 16th-century [[Jacobean architecture|Jacobean]] mansion with a symmetrical front and square towers, set within the older castle walls and overlooked by the keep above.<ref>Garnett, pp.5, 31; Lyte (1909), p.365.</ref> The building was decorated in the latest styles, including ornamental plaster ceilings.<ref>Lyte (1909), p.365.</ref> The project ran almost three times over budget, costing Luttrell more than £1,200.<ref name="GarnettP31" />{{#tag:ref|It is difficult to accurately compare 17th-century and modern prices or incomes. £1,200 could equate to between £171,000 to £2,140,000, depending on the measure used.<ref>''[http://www.measuringworth.com/ukcompare/ Five Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a UK Pound Amount, 1830 to Present]'', Lawrence H. Officer, MeasuringWorth, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref>|group="nb"}}

===English Civil War and the Restoration===
[[File:Dunster Castle gate.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.8|Original 13th-century gate, bound in iron]]

When the [[First English Civil War]] began in August 1642, George's eldest son [[Thomas Luttrell (1583–1644)|Thomas]] supported [[Parliament of England|Parliament]]; [[William Russell, 1st Duke of Bedford]] and [[Roundhead|Parliamentarian]] commander in Devon and Somerset, ordered him to strengthen the garrison at Dunster.<ref name="carterP2">Carter, p.2.</ref> The local [[Cavalier|Royalist]] commander [[William Seymour, 2nd Duke of Somerset]], attacked the castle in 1642 but was repulsed by the garrison, led by Thomas' wife Jane.<ref name=GarnettP40>Garnett, p.40.</ref> In early 1643, the war in the south-west turned in favour of the King, and on 7 June 1643 the Royalists assaulted the castle again and Luttrell switched sides.<ref name=carterP2/> Colonel [[Sir Francis Wyndham, 1st Baronet|Francis  Wyndham]] was appointed Royalist governor,<ref name=carterP2/> and the future [[Charles II of England|Charles II]] stayed at the castle in May 1645.<ref>Garnett, p.45.</ref>

During 1645 the Royalist military cause largely collapsed, and Colonel [[Robert Blake (admiral)|Robert Blake]] led a Parliamentarian force against Dunster in October.<ref name=GarnettCarterP40/> In November, Blake established his artillery in the village and began digging mines beneath the castle walls.<ref name=GarnettP40/> Dunster was briefly relieved in February 1646 but the siege resumed, and by April the Royalist position was untenable; Wyndham negotiated an honourable surrender and a Parliamentarian garrison installed.<ref name=GarnettCarterP40>Garnett, p.40; Carter, p.3.</ref> After the end of the [[Second English Civil War]] in 1649, Parliament decided to deliberately destroy, or [[slighting|slight]], the defences of castles in key Royalist areas, including the south-west.<ref>Thompson, p.154.</ref>

Thomas Luttrell had died in February 1644 and his son George Luttrell convinced the authorities to destroy only the medieval defensive walls, rather than the entire castle, leaving Dunster damaged from the recent siege but still habitable; the walls were demolished over 12 days in August 1650 by a team of 300 workmen.<ref>Garnett, pp.40–41; Thompson, p.156; Lyte (1909), p.367.</ref> The only parts of the medieval walls to survive were the Great Gatehouse and the bases of the two towers in the Lower Ward.<ref>Carter, p.3; Garnett, p.31.</ref> George Luttrell died without children, and Dunster Castle passed to his brother [[Francis Luttrell (1628–1666)|Francis]], who survived the political turmoil of the [[Commonwealth of England|Commonwealth]] prior to the 1660 [[Stuart Restoration]].<ref name=GarnettP41/>

Francis died in 1666 and the castle in 1670 passed to his second son, another [[Francis Luttrell (1659–1690)|Francis]]. He married Mary Tregonwell, a wealthy heiress worth £2,500 a year, and used her income to modernise the castle during the 1680s, including a grand staircase in the latest style.<ref>Garnett, p.41; Lyte (1909), p.368; price ref.</ref> As a colonel in the local militia, during the November 1688 [[Glorious Revolution]] Francis backed the removal of [[James II of England|James II]] by his son-in-law [[William III of England|William of Orange]]; when William landed in Devon, Francis mustered a number of companies of infantry at Dunster on 19 November to support him, which formed the basis for the later [[Green Howards]] regiment.<ref name=GarnettP41>Garnett, p.41.</ref> During this period the castle still kept an armoury of 43 [[musket]]s.<ref name=NatTrustArts>''[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-february-2011.pdf National Trust Arts, Buildings, Collections Bulletin, February 2011]'', p.3, (PDF) Felicity Baber and Brian Godwin, the National Trust, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> Francis died heavily in debt in 1690, and his widow Mary moved the contents of the castle to London, where they were destroyed in a fire in 1696.<ref name=GarnettP41/>

===18th century===
[[File:Dunster Castle 1733.jpg|thumb|upright=1.9|The castle in 1733, showing the then recently planted New Way, the mansion (l), Great Gatehouse (c) and stables (r). The motte, with the summer house, is visible in the background]]
At the start of the 18th century the Luttrells and Dunster Castle faced many financial challenges.<ref name=GarnettP42>Garnett, p.42.</ref> Francis's son [[Alexander Luttrell (1663–1711)|Alexander]], inherited the castle when he came of age in 1704, but it was still mostly empty and carried large debts with it.<ref name=GarnettP42/> Alexander died young in 1711 and his widow, Dorothy, spent almost twenty years paying off the debts.<ref name=GarnettP42/> Dorothy built a new chapel, designed by Sir [[James Thornhill]] in white [[Portland stone]], on the rear of the mansion at a cost of £1,300 (£178,000 at 2009 prices); few records of this remain, but the interior probably resembled that of the chapel at [[Wimpole Hall]].<ref>Garnett, pp.31, 41, Lyte (1909), p.373; ''[http://www.measuringworth.com/ukcompare/ Five Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a UK Pound Amount, 1830 to Present]'', Lawrence H. Officer, MeasuringWorth, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> A safer, if less grand, approach road to the castle was created, called the New Way, and the remains of the Upper Ward on top of the motte were flattened to be used as a [[bowling green]], complete with an octagonal [[summer house]].<ref>Garnett, p.31; Lyte (1909), pp.372–373.</ref> Dorothy's son, [[Alexander Luttrell (1705–1737)|Alexander Luttrell]], took over the castle in 1726 but ran up new debts, and the castle was handed over into the control of a [[receivership|receiver]].<ref name=GarnettP42/>

[[Henry Fownes Luttrell (died 1780)|Henry Fownes Luttrell]], who married [[Margaret Fownes-Luttrell|Margaret]], Alexander's daughter, and took the Luttrell name, moved to Dunster in 1747.<ref>Garnett, p.42; ''[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wra-1356327562038/770124/ Dunster Castle's portraits of noteworthy Luttrells: Margaret and Henry Fownes Luttrell (m.1747)]'', the National Trust, accessed 12 March 2015.</ref> The couple redesigned and redecorated the castle in a [[Rococo architecture|Rococo]] style, including the extensive use of the recently invented and highly fashionable [[wallpaper]].<ref>Garnett, p.42; Lyte (1909), p.376.</ref> Henry Luttrell raised the ground height of the Lower Ward between 1764 and 1765 to extend the New Way all around to the front of his mansion, adding additional ornamental towers onto the inside of the Great Gatehouse in the process.<ref>Emery, p.677; Lyte (1909), pp.378–379.</ref> A [[folly]], [[Conygar Tower]], was constructed by architect [[Richard Phelps (artist)|Richard Phelps]] to improve the view from the castle, and a larger park of 141 hectares (348 acres) was built just to the south of the castle, requiring the eviction of a number of tenant farmers.<ref>Garnett, pp.27, 29.</ref>

===19th and 20th centuries===
[[File:Justice Room, Dunster Castle.jpg|thumb|left|The Justice's Desk in the Justice Room{{#tag:ref|The Justice Room and the Desk are named after George Luttrell's role as a [[Justice of the Peace]].<ref>Garnett, p.21.</ref>|group="nb"}}]]
Henry's son, John, inherited the castle in 1780, but when his son, also called John, inherited in 1816 he chose to live in London instead, opening up Dunster Castle to the public.<ref>Garnett, pp.44, 48.</ref> By 1845 the castle appeared to visitors to be past its prime: with only two of John's sisters living there and no horses or hunting dogs left in the castle grounds, the remaining servants had little to do.<ref name=GarnettP44>Garnett, p.44.</ref> John's brother Henry inherited in 1857, but he too lived in London rather than at Dunster.<ref name=GarnettP44/>

George Luttrell inherited the castle in 1867 and began an extensive modernisation, backed by the considerable income from the Dunster estates – in a period of agricultural [[Boom and bust|boom]] in England, the estates were producing £22,000 in revenue a year (£1.49 million at 2010 prices).<ref>Garnett, p.44; ''[http://www.measuringworth.com/ukcompare/ Five Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a UK Pound Amount, 1830 to Present]'', Lawrence H. Officer, MeasuringWorth, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> It was fashionable during the [[Victorian era|mid-Victorian]] period to remodel existing castles to produce what was felt to be a more consistent Gothic or sometimes Picturesque appearance and George, a keen historian, decided to follow this trend at Dunster; in the process, he also hoped to accommodate the larger household and facilities required for a 19th-century landowner: by 1881, the castle required 15 "living-in" servants alone.<ref>Garnett, pp.32, 35.</ref> He employed [[Anthony Salvin]], a noted architect then most famous for his work at [[Alnwick Castle]], to carry out the work between 1868 and 1872 at a total cost of £25,350 (equivalent to £1.76 million in 2010).<ref>Garnett, p.32; ''[http://www.measuringworth.com/ukcompare/ Five Ways to Compute the Relative Value of a UK Pound Amount, 1830 to Present]'', Lawrence H. Officer, MeasuringWorth, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> The work included the construction of an underground [[reservoir]], holding {{convert|40000|impgal|L|abbr=off}} of water to provide running water for the castle and village.<ref name=BBCReservoir>''[https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-35209407 Dunster Castle to open underground Victorian reservoir]'', BBC News, accessed 1 January 2016; ''[http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=MSO10036-Reservoir-Dunster-Castle-(Monument) MSO10036 - Reservoir, Dunster Castle]'', Exmoor National Park, accessed 1 January 2016.</ref>

Salvin aimed to create a castle that would appear to have grown up organically over time, but still appeal to Victorian aesthetic taste. Accordingly, a large, square tower was built on the west side of the castle and another smaller tower on the east, both creating additional space but also making the castle deliberately asymmetrical.<ref>Garnett, pp.32–33.</ref> The 18th-century chapel at the rear was demolished and replaced with another tower, alongside a modern [[Conservatory (greenhouse)|conservatory]].<ref name=GarnettP33>Garnett, p.33.</ref> A variety of windows in the styles of different historical periods were inserted in the walls, while modern Victorian technology, including [[gas lighting]]-supported by a [[Coal gas|gas]] [[Process manufacturing|plant]] in the basement-central heating and new kitchens were installed within the castle.<ref name=GarnettP33/> The roof of the Great Gatehouse was raised to create a more uniform sequence of battlements, and a large hall for gatherings of the local farmers installed.<ref>Emery, p.677; Garnett, p.27.</ref> A new wing of servants' quarters and offices were sunk into the hill, spread over two floors leading away from the main part of the mansion.<ref>Garnett, p.36.</ref>

[[File:Plan of Dunster Castle, post-1860s.png|thumb|300px|right|Plan of the castle, after 1872: A - Dining Room; B – Service rooms and stairway to servants' wing; C – Inner Hall; D – Entrance Lobby; E – Outer Hall; F – Drawing Room; G – Billiard Room; H – Conservatory; I – Justice Room; J – Library]]
Internally, Salvin knocked through existing rooms to create the Outer Hall, a new gallery on the first floor, a [[Cue sports|billiard]] room, a new library and a drawing room.<ref>Garnett, p.6, 16, 21–24.</ref> Much of the wooden 17th-century panelling in the parlour and the hall had to be stripped out as part of the renovations.<ref>Lyte (1909), p.382.</ref> As part of his work, Salvin appears to have used a number of rolled [[wrought-iron]] beams to span the resulting structural gaps in the building, an advanced use of that technology for the time.<ref>''[http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/catalogue/adsdata/arch-954-1/dissemination/pdf/michaelh1-61588_1.pdf Dunster Castle Roof Repairs 2006–2008]'', p.17, (PDF) Michael Heaton Heritage Consultants, accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> The house was refurnished with newly bought 16th and 17th-century artwork, two [[brass]] Italian [[cannon]]s and a stuffed [[polar bear]].<ref>Lyte (1909), p.382; Garnett, p.6.</ref>

Alexander Luttrell, who inherited Dunster Castle in 1910, chose to live at East Quantoxhead instead, and it was left empty until his son Geoffrey reoccupied the castle in 1920, redecorating some of the rooms in a contemporary style and building a [[polo]] ground alongside the castle.<ref>Garnett, pp.29, 33, 46.</ref> The castle and the surrounding countryside at this time was very popular with the Luttrells for [[fox hunting]] and [[shooting]].<ref name=NatTrustArts/> During the Second World War the castle was used as a convalescent home for injured naval and American officers between 1943 and 1944.<ref name=GarnettP47>Garnett, p.47.</ref>

Alexander died in 1944, and the [[Inheritance tax|death duties]] proved crippling to Geoffrey. In 1949 he sold the castle and 3,480 hectares (8,600 acres) of the lands to the Ashdale Property Company, retaining a tenancy of the castle for himself.<ref name=GarnettP47/> The [[Crown Estate]] bought the estate from Ashdale and sold the castle back to Geoffrey in 1954.<ref name=GarnettP47/> His son Colonel Sir [[Walter Luttrell]] lived away from Dunster, and following the death of his mother – the last Luttrell to live in the property – gave the castle and most of its contents to the [[National Trust]] in 1976.<ref name=GarnettP47/>

==Today==
[[File:Dunster Castle frontage.jpg|thumb|300px|The castle in 2011, showing the Great Gatehouse (l) and the main body of the castle (r)]]
Dunster Castle is operated by the National Trust as a [[tourist attraction]]. Little remains of the medieval castle except for the Great Gatehouse and the remains of several towers in the Lower Ward; the heart of the modern castle today is the much altered 17th-century manor house.<ref>Emery, p.677.</ref> The key features of the castle include the original 13th-century gates and several pieces of art, including a Tudor copy of [[Hans Eworth]]'s famous [[John Luttrell (picture)|allegorical portrait of Sir John Luttrell]], and a sequence of leather [[tapestry|tapestries]] showing scenes from the story of [[Antony and Cleopatra]].<ref>Garnett, pp.9, 16–17, 30.</ref> The castle also holds a piano that once belonged to the composer [[Vivian Ellis]].<ref>Garnett, p.13.</ref> The gardens surrounding the castle cover approximately {{convert|6|ha|acre|0}} and include the [[National Plant Collection]] of [[Arbutus unedo|Strawberry Trees]]; the wider parkland beyond totals {{convert|277|ha|acre|0}}.<ref>''[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-vh/w-visits/w-findaplace/w-dunstercastle/w-dunstercastle-garden.htm Explore the Garden]'', [[National Trust]], accessed 24 September 2011; ''[http://www.parksandgardens.org/places-and-people/site/1187 Dunster Castle]'', Parks and Gardens UK, Parks and Gardens Data Services Ltd., accessed 9 July 2011.</ref>

Just to the south of the castle is the restored 18th-century [[Dunster Working Watermill|castle watermill]].<ref>Garnett, p.28.</ref> In 2017 the castle received 209,245 visitors.<ref>''[http://www.alva.org.uk/details.cfm?p=423 Latest Visitor Figures]'', Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, accessed 18 May 2018.</ref> Dunster Castle has been designated as a Grade I [[listed building]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=DUNSTER CASTLE AND GATEHOUSE, Dunster - 1057643 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1057643 |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref> and [[Scheduled Monument]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Motte and bailey at Dunster Castle, Dunster - 1020410 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1020410 |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref> The grounds are included on [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]] at Grade II*.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DUNSTER CASTLE, Carhampton - 1000467 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000467 |access-date=2022-06-06 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref> The castle has required continuing maintenance work, in particular to its roof, itself an important historical feature. Efforts have been made to gradually redecorate the castle in a period style, using reproductions of original wallpapers and materials.<ref>''[http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/catalogue/adsdata/arch-954-1/dissemination/pdf/michaelh1-61588_1.pdf Dunster Castle Roof Repairs 2006–2008]'', (PDF) pp.4, 15, Michael Heaton Heritage Consultants, accessed 24 September 2011; Garnett, pp.21, 15.</ref> The National Trust installed solar panels behind the battlements on the roof in 2008 to provide electricity and make the premises more environmentally friendly. This was the first time the National Trust have taken this approach to a Grade I listed building, and it is expected to save 1,714 kg (3,778 lb) of [[carbon]] a year.<ref>''[https://www.theguardian.com/uk/2008/feb/07/artnews.art The 1,000-year-old Castle Fighting Climate Change]'', Steven Morris, 7 February 2008, ''[[The Guardian]]'', accessed 24 September 2011; ''[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/nt_ecs_ext_dun_volt_final.pdf Sustainable Technology Case Study]'', (PDF) [[National Trust]], accessed 24 September 2011.</ref> In 2015, the National Trust announced plans to make the 19th-century reservoir open to the public,<ref name=BBCReservoir/> and the reservoir was formally opened for viewing in April 2016.<ref>{{cite news |title=Dunster Castle unveils underground Victorian reservoir |url=https://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/news/14437016.dunster-castle-unveils-underground-victorian-reservoir/ |access-date=11 May 2019 |work=Somerset County Gazette |date=19 April 2016}}</ref>

'''Dunster Working Watermill''' (also known as Castle Mill) is a restored 18th century [[watermill]], situated on the [[River Avill]], close to [[Gallox Bridge, Dunster|Gallox Bridge]], in the grounds of [[Dunster Castle]] in [[Dunster]], [[Somerset]], England. It is a Grade II* [[Listed building (United Kingdom)|listed building]]<ref name=nhle>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1173447 |desc=Castle Mill and attached gateway and gates|access-date=5 April 2015}}</ref> and within the Grade II* [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of Special Historic Interest in England|registered parkland]] of the castle.<ref>{{Cite web |title=DUNSTER CASTLE, Carhampton - 1000467 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1000467 |access-date=2023-05-03 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref>

The mill stands on a site where a mill was first recorded in the [[Domesday Book]], but the present building was constructed around 1780. It closed in 1962 but was restored in 1979 and is still used to grind flour. The equipment is powered by two [[Water wheel#Overshot wheel|overshot wheels]]. It is owned and run by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].

== History ==

At the time of the [[Domesday Book]] in 1086 there were two mills in Dunster. One which was called the Lower Mill was on the site of the present mill. In the 17th century there were both malt and oats mills but by 1721 one of these had been converted to a [[fulling]] mill.<ref name=vch>{{cite web|title=Dunster: Economic History|url=http://www.victoriacountyhistory.ac.uk/sites/default/files/work-in-progress/dunster_economic_history_1st_draft_edited.pdf|publisher=Victoria County Histories|access-date=8 February 2014|pages=27–31}}</ref> The present mill, which was built around 1780 and replaced the two former mills.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dunster Working Watermill|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-dunsterworkingwatermill|publisher=National Trust|access-date=23 September 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629101548/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-dunsterworkingwatermill|archive-date=29 June 2011}}</ref> In 1940 a bakery was added.<ref name=vch/> The mill ground corn until [[World War II]] and then animal feed until it closed in 1962.<ref name=conservationarea>{{cite web|title=Dunster Conservation Area Character Appraisal|url=http://www.dartmoor-npa.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0013/127111/Dunster.pdf|publisher=Exmoor National Park Authority|access-date=8 February 2014|page=20|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222061140/http://www.dartmoor-npa.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0013/127111/Dunster.pdf|archive-date=22 February 2014}}</ref>

It was restored to working order in 1979,<ref name=ee>{{cite web|title=Dunster Working Water Mill |url=http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=345 |publisher=Everything Exmoor |access-date=25 January 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140912104621/http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=345 |archive-date=12 September 2014 }}</ref> winning a conservation award in 1982.<ref name=conservationarea/> The mill still produces Wheat, Rye and Spelt flour from organic grain.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dunster Water Mill|url=http://www.dunsterwatermill.co.uk/index.htm|publisher=Dunster Water Mill|access-date=23 September 2011|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110823103558/http://www.dunsterwatermill.co.uk/index.htm|archive-date=23 August 2011}}</ref> A cafe was opened in the buildings which used to be the wagon house and stables.<ref name=vch/> Further restoration work, completed in 2007, was funded by the Exmoor Sustainable Development Fund.<ref name=ee/><ref>{{cite news|last1=Alder|first1=Chris|title=Dunster's water mill gets a facelift|url=http://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/news/west_somerset_news/1632102.Dunster_s_water_mill_gets_a_facelift/|access-date=25 January 2015|work=Somerset County Gazette|date=21 August 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304122907/http://www.somersetcountygazette.co.uk/news/west_somerset_news/1632102.Dunster_s_water_mill_gets_a_facelift/|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

It is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and can be visited by National Trust members for free or by non-members buying an entry ticket.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dunster Working Watermill|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dunster-working-watermill/visitor-information/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=9 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131225042303/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dunster-working-watermill/visitor-information/|archive-date=25 December 2013|url-status=live}}</ref> The site is visited by around 60,000 tourists a year and produces around 10 tonnes of flour each year.<ref name=ee/><ref>{{cite web|title=Dunster Water Mill|url=http://windmills.org.uk/industrial-archaeology/water-mills/somerset/dunster-water-mill/|publisher=Windmills UK|access-date=25 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150416232218/http://windmills.org.uk/industrial-archaeology/water-mills/somerset/dunster-water-mill/|archive-date=16 April 2015|url-status=live}}</ref> The second (Lower) waterwheel was replaced in 2015 and the associated machinery was refurbished and repaired in 2016.  The 3 French burr millstones were dressed in 2024.<ref>{{cite web|title=Rare 18th Century two-wheeled waterwheel restored in Somerset|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-33595870|publisher=BBC|access-date=21 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150721053457/http://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-somerset-33595870|archive-date=21 July 2015|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Architecture and machinery ==
[[File:Dunster Mill (geograph 2455304).jpg|thumb|left|The pit wheel and spur wheel along with flour transporter and flour sieve.]]
The three-storey building has a slate roof. To the south east a stone wall contains [[wrought iron]] gates in an arched gateway.<ref name=nhle/>

The milling equipment is powered by a pair of [[Water wheel#Overshot wheel|overshot waterwheels]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Castle Mill and attached gateway and gates, Dunster|url=http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=MSO9458-Castle-Mill-and-attached-gateway-and-gates-Dunster|work=Exmoor Historic Environment Record|publisher=Exmoor National Park|access-date=28 November 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141204212442/http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=MSO9458-Castle-Mill-and-attached-gateway-and-gates-Dunster|archive-date=4 December 2014|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Dunster Castle Mill|url=http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=36933|work=Pastscape|publisher=English Heritage|access-date=8 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222170449/http://www.pastscape.org.uk/hob.aspx?hob_id=36933|archive-date=22 February 2014|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Maintenance Works, Dunster Watermill|url=http://www.dorothearestorations.com/case-studies/maintenance-works-dunster-watermill|publisher=Dorothea Restorations|access-date=25 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160306062310/http://www.dorothearestorations.com/case-studies/maintenance-works-dunster-watermill|archive-date=6 March 2016|url-status=live}}</ref> which transfer power to associated (internal) pit wheel, spur wheel and stone nut. This then drives the millstones. There are trapdoors on the first and second floors to allow grain to be hoisted up the building via the sack hoist.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Fishar|first1=John|title=Dunster|url=http://www.dartmoor-npa.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0013/127111/Dunster.pdf|website=Dartmoor National Park|publisher=Exmoor National Park Authority|access-date=25 January 2015|page=20|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222061140/http://www.dartmoor-npa.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0013/127111/Dunster.pdf|archive-date=22 February 2014}}</ref>

'''Fyne Court''' is a [[National Trust]]-owned [[nature reserve]] and [[visitor centre]] in [[Broomfield, Somerset]], England. It was formerly an estate, and large [[English country house]], belonging to the Crosse family.

[[Andrew Crosse]] conducted a series of experiments with electricity, including the development of large [[voltaic pile]]s, at the house during his ownership in the early 19th century. The main building of Fyne Court burnt down in 1894. The buildings which survived the fire have been used as offices and a visitor centre by organisations such as the [[Somerset Wildlife Trust]] and [[Quantock Hills]] [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]] Service since it came into the ownership of the National Trust in 1967. It is surrounded by a large country estate of woodland, ponds and meadows. Within the grounds are a [[folly]] and boathouse.

==History==
[[File:Andrew Crosse.jpg|thumb|left|upright|[[Andrew Crosse]]]]
The nature reserve is set in parkland which was originally the pleasure grounds of a large house belonging to 19th-century scientist and pioneer in electricity, [[Andrew Crosse]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Fyne Court|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/fyne-court/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=22 January 2015}}</ref> His family had owned the house from its construction, Fyne Court having been built in around 1629 by an earlier Andrew Crosse, who had purchased part of the manor of Broomfield.<ref name=greswell>{{cite book |title=
Dumnonia and the Valley of the Parret: A Historical Retrospect |first=William |last=greswell |year=1922 |publisher=Barnicott & Pearce |page=175}}</ref><ref name="bush">{{cite book |title=Somerset: The complete guide |last=Bush |first=Robin |author-link=Robin Bush (historian) |year=1994 |publisher=Dovecote Press |location=Wimborne, Dorset |isbn=1-874336-26-1 |url=https://archive.org/details/somersetcomplete0000bush/page/46 |page=[https://archive.org/details/somersetcomplete0000bush/page/46 46] }}</ref> The house had been enlarged and extensively remodelled by Andrew Crosse (1704–66), great-uncle of the scientist, who also completed a fashionable [[Arcadia (utopia)|Arcadian]] garden including five linked ponds, a serpentine lake, and additional tree planting.

Having lost his parents, his father in 1800 and his mother in 1805, Crosse took over the management of the family estates at the age of 21. Among his experiments Crosse erected "an extensive apparatus for examining the electricity of the atmosphere," incorporating at one point an insulated wire some {{convert|1.25|mi|km}} long, later shortened to {{convert|1800|ft|m}}, suspended from poles and trees. Using this wire he was able to determine the polarity of the atmosphere under various weather conditions. His results were published by his friend [[George Singer]] in 1814, as part of Singer's ''Elements of Electricity and Electro-Chemistry''.<ref name=memoirs>{{cite book |title=Memorials scientific and literary of Andrew Cross, the electrician |last=Crosse |first=Cornelia A H |year=1857 |publisher=Longman, Brown, Green, Longmans and Robert |location=London }}</ref>

Along with Sir [[Humphry Davy]] (who visited Fyne Court in 1827), Crosse was one of the first to develop large [[voltaic pile]]s.<ref>Encyclopædia Britannica, 1911 edition, Volume V09, Page 185</ref> Although it was not the largest he built, [[Henry Minchin Noad]]'s ''Manual of Electricity'' describes a battery consisting of 50 jars containing {{convert|73|sqft|m2}} of coated surface. Using his wires Crosse was able to charge and discharge it some 20 times a minute, "accompanied by reports almost as loud as those of a cannon".<ref name=memoirs /> He became known locally as "the thunder and lightning man".<ref>{{cite web|title=Andrew Crosse: The man and the myth|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wra-1356292904077/369643/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=22 January 2015}}</ref> In 1836 Sir Richard Phillips described seeing a wide variety of voltaic piles at Fyne Court, totalling 2,500, of which 1,500 were in use when he visited.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Andrew Crosse : Early nineteenth-century amateur of electrical science |author=Pocock RF |journal=IEE Proceedings A |volume=140 |number=3 |date=May 1993}}</ref>
[[File:Susan Harris (née Hamilton), Countess of Malmesbury (1854-1935).jpg|thumb|Susan Harris (née Hamilton), Countess of Malmesbury (1854–1935)]]
The house was the childhood home of Susan Harris, Countess of Malmesbury, who was the daughter of John Hamilton of Fyne Court and the second wife of [[James Harris, 3rd Earl of Malmesbury]], [[Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)|Foreign Secretary]] and [[Conservative Party (United Kingdom)|Conservative]] politician. She published a number of books and articles in her lifetime including 'Village Life in England' in which she recorded some reminiscences of life in Broomfield.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Malmesbury|first1=Susan H.|title=Village Life in England|date=1894|publisher=University of Northern Iowa|pages=304–311|jstor=25103295}}</ref> She later married Major General Sir [[John Charles Ardagh]] who is buried in [[Church of St Mary & All Saints, Broomfield]] churchyard and wrote an account of his life.

The house burnt down in 1894.<ref name=nthistory>{{cite web|title=Fyne Court History|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/fyne-court/history/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=9 February 2014}}</ref><ref  name="waite">{{cite book |title=Portrait of the Quantocks |last=Waite |first=Vincent |year=1964 |publisher=Robert Hale |location=London |isbn=0-7091-1158-4 |pages=38–42 }}</ref> However the detached music room in which Crosse conducted his experiments survived,<ref>{{cite web|title=Fire at Fyne Court|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/wra-1356292904077/369670/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=9 February 2014}}</ref> along with some of the books and oil paintings by [[Anthony van Dyck]] and [[Peter Paul Rubens]].<ref>{{cite news|title=The Destruction by Fire of Fyne Court, Bridgwater|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000264/18940904/014/0003|work=Western Daily Press|date=4 September 1894| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The laboratory table on which Crosse carried out experiments stands in the aisle of the [[Church of St Mary & All Saints, Broomfield|Church of St. Mary and All Saints in Broomfield]] and an [[obelisk]] in his memory is in the churchyard.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1058934 |title=Church of St. Mary and All Saints |access-date=9 March 2008 |work=historicengland.org.uk |df=dmy }}</ref>

In 1918 several hundred acres of the woodland within the park was sold at an auction in [[Taunton]].<ref>{{cite news|title=The Fyne Court Estate|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000527/19181113/041/0004|work=Taunton Courier, and Western Advertiser|date=13 November 1918| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Fyne Court was left to the [[National Trust]] by John Adams in 1967, and passed in to the Trust's ownership in 1972 once legal issues were resolved.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Wright|first1=Brian|title=Andrew Crosse and the mite that shocked the world: The life and work of an electrical pioneer|page=284|isbn=9781784624385|date=2015|publisher=Troubador}}</ref> It was also used as the headquarters of the [[Somerset Wildlife Trust]].<ref name=qonline>{{cite web|title=Broomfield|url=http://www.quantockonline.co.uk/quantocks/villages/broomfield/broomfield1.html|publisher=Quantock Online|access-date=29 August 2011}}</ref>  The [[Quantock Hills]] [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty|AONB]] Service have their headquarters in the grounds.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fyne Court|url=http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=458|publisher=Exmoor Encyclopedia|access-date=22 January 2015}}</ref>

==Grounds==
[[File:A folly at Fyne Court (geograph 2053192).jpg|thumb|The folly|left]]
Fyne Court is surrounded by a {{convert|65|acre|m2|adj=on}} estate.<ref>{{cite web|title=Acquisitions up to December 2011 |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheader=application%2Fpdf&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=MDT-Type&blobheadername3=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B+filename%3D297%252F965%252Fnt_acquisitions_dec2011-2%252C2.pdf&blobheadervalue2=abinary%3B+charset%3DUTF-8&blobheadervalue3=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1349117284549&ssbinary=true |publisher=National Trust |access-date=19 April 2015 |page=13 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714144751/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheader=application%2Fpdf&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=MDT-Type&blobheadername3=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B%2Bfilename%3D297%2F965%2Fnt_acquisitions_dec2011-2%2C2.pdf&blobheadervalue2=abinary%3B%2Bcharset%3DUTF-8&blobheadervalue3=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1349117284549&ssbinary=true |archive-date=14 July 2014 |df=dmy }}</ref>
Much of the landscaping, including an arboretum laid out in 1780, has become overgrown and now provides varied habitats including broadleaved woodland, ponds and meadows grazed by highland cattle.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fyne Court|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/fyne-court/wildlife/|work=Wildlife|publisher=National Trust|access-date=22 January 2015}}</ref>  The site is home to over 100 species of fungi and some rare invertebrates.<ref name=qonline/> In the grounds is a [[folly]] with two {{convert|4|m|ft|order=flip}} wide [[crenelated]] towers, and a boathouse.<ref>{{cite book|last=Holt|first=Jonathan|title=Somerset Follies|year=2007|publisher=Akeman Press|location=Bath|isbn=9780954613877|pages=54–55}}</ref>

5919118.title: Dolebury Warren
5919118.extract:
Dolebury Warren (also known as Dolebury Camp) is a 90.6-hectare (224-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and ancient monument near the villages of Churchill and Rowberrow in North Somerset, part of South West England. It is owned by the National Trust, who acquired the freehold in 1983, and managed by the Avon Wildlife Trust.
Standing on a limestone ridge on the northern edge of the Mendip Hills, it was made into a hill fort during the Iron Age and was occupied into the Roman period. The extensive fort covers 9.1 hectares (22 acres) with single or double defensive ramparts around it. The name Dolebury Warren comes from its use during the medieval or post medieval periods as a rabbit warren. The topography and differing soil types provide a habitat for an unusually wide range of plants, attracting a variety of insects, including several species of butterfly.

'''Dolebury Warren''' (also known as '''Dolebury Camp''') is a {{convert|90.6|ha|adj=on}} [[biological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI) and [[ancient monument]] near the villages of [[Churchill, Somerset|Churchill]] and [[Rowberrow]] in [[North Somerset]], part of [[South West England]]. It is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]], who acquired the freehold in 1983, and managed by the [[Avon Wildlife Trust]].

Standing on a [[limestone]] ridge on the northern edge of the [[Mendip Hills]], it was made into a [[hill fort]] during the [[Iron Age]] and was occupied into the [[Roman Britain|Roman]] period. The extensive fort covers {{convert|9.1|ha}} with single or double [[Defensive wall|defensive ramparts]] around it. The name Dolebury Warren comes from its use during the medieval or post medieval periods as a rabbit [[warren (domestic)|warren]]. The [[topography]] and [[pedodiversity|differing soil types]] provide a habitat for an unusually wide range of plants, attracting a variety of insects, including several species of butterfly.

==Geology and location==

The site is at the top of a [[Carboniferous Limestone]] ridge on the northern edge of the [[Mendip Hills]]. It forms part of the [[Black Down, Somerset|Black Down]] [[Pericline]] where the limestone has been exposed because of erosion of the overlying [[Triassic]] [[Dolomite (rock)|dolomitic]] [[Conglomerate (geology)|conglomerate]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Banwell to Churchill|url=http://www.bgs.ac.uk/mendips/localities/banwell.html|publisher=British Geological Survey|access-date=23 August 2014}}</ref>{{sfn|Farrant|2008|p=47}} The soil depth varies considerably, owing to the slope within the site and the effects of its exposure to the wind.{{sfn|Atthill|1976|p = 42}}

Dolebury Warren overlooks the villages of [[Churchill, Somerset|Churchill]] and [[Rowberrow]] and provides good visibility across the surrounding lower lying areas as far as the [[Bristol Channel]]. The highest point, at the eastern end of the site is {{convert|183|m}} [[Ordnance datum|OD]], with the hillfort being up to {{convert|50|m}} below this.{{sfn|Bowden|2009|pp=1–3}} It is the starting point for the [[Limestone Link]], a {{convert|36|mi|km|0|adj=on}} [[Long-distance footpaths in the United Kingdom|long-distance footpath]] which ends at [[Cold Ashton]] in [[Gloucestershire]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Limestone Link (Cotswolds to Mendips)|url=https://www.ldwa.org.uk/ldp/members/show_path.php?path_name=Limestone+Link+%28Cotswolds+to+Mendips%29|publisher=Long Distance Walkers Association|access-date=24 August 2014}}</ref>

== Description ==
The fort covers an area of {{convert|9.1|ha}} and commands views over the surrounding countryside.{{sfn|Dyer|2001|p = 156}} The hill fort is [[Hill fort#Types of hill fort|bivallate]] on three sides and a single [[Rampart (fortification)|rampart]] on the southern side which is protected by a steep slope.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dolebury Camp Hillfort, Somerset|date=27 November 2013 |url=http://digitaldigging.net/dolebury-camp-hill-fort-somerset/|publisher=Digital Digging|access-date=23 August 2014}}</ref> It is almost rectangular with the longest axis from east to west being {{convert|487|m}} long and {{convert|200|m}} from north to south, surrounded by a rampart which is around {{convert|4|m}} high and {{convert|12|m}} wide.<ref name="nhle" /> It was protected by a [[limestone]] [[defensive wall|rampart]] with a ditch and [[counterscarp]] on all sides but the south. There is an inturned entrance on the west and an annexe of {{convert|0.4|ha}} protecting the easier eastern approach.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dolebury |work=Roman Britain |url=http://www.roman-britain.org/celtic/dolebury.htm |access-date=14 November 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100613162359/http://roman-britain.org/celtic/dolebury.htm |archive-date=13 June 2010 }}</ref>

==History==

=== Etymology ===
The name Dolebury may mean ''the idol hill'' from the [[Old English]] ''dwol'' and ''beorg''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Robinson |first=Stephen |title=Somerset Place Names |year=1992 |publisher=The Dovecote Press Ltd |location=Wimbourne |isbn=978-1-874336-03-7|page=56}}</ref>

===Early===

[[File:Dolebury Camp Somerset Map.jpg|thumb|right|Earthworks at Dolebury Warren]]

[[File:Dolebury Hillfort southern ramparts - geograph.org.uk - 593107.jpg|thumb|right|The southern ramparts]]

Various artefacts have been uncovered representing the long period of occupation of the site at Dolebury Warren. These include flintwork from the [[Palaeolithic]], bronze spearheads, Bronze Age pottery, and [[Roman Britain|Roman]] pottery and coins.<ref name="nhle" />{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 3}} There is evidence of occupation of the site during the [[Iron Age]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Mendip Hills An Archaeological Survey of the Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty | work=Somerset County Council Archeological Projects | url=http://www1.somerset.gov.uk/archives/hes/downloads/HES_MendipAONB.pdf| access-date=16 January 2011}}</ref> The defences and [[Celts|Celtic]] field systems there date back to the 7th century−3rd century [[Common Era|BCE]], though they might mask earlier developments.<ref>{{cite web | title=Tower Head and Dolebury Warren | work=Isle of Avalon | url=https://www.isleofavalon.co.uk/sacredsites/towerhead.html | access-date=28 October 2006}}</ref>{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 13}} The hillfort was occupied until approximately 100BC, though it is possible that it was reoccupied in the Roman and post-Roman periods.{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 13}} The archeological consultant Peter Leach has suggested there may even have been a Roman Temple built within the hillfort,{{sfn|Leach|2001|p = 100}} while aerial photographs suggest the probable remains of an Iron Age or Roman coaxial field system.<ref>{{PastScape|mnumber=1494935|access-date=24 August 2014}}</ref>{{sfn|Aston|Burrow|1991|p = 85}} Local historian Robin Atthill also suggests that Dolebury may have re-emerged as an important centre of population in the 5th century.{{sfn|Atthill|1976|p = 73}}[[File:Dolebury Iron Age Hillfort - geograph.org.uk - 593105.jpg|thumb|left|Looking east towards the highest point]]

===Medieval===
In the medieval or post-medieval period, the remains of the hillfort were used as a [[Warren (domestic)|rabbit warren]] which was used to breed rabbits, providing valuable meat and fur. Many warrens were surrounded by banks or walls to prevent the rabbits from escaping; escaped rabbits caused damage to nearby farmland and meant a loss in profit.{{sfn|Williamson|2006}} The warren at Dolebury is completely enclosed by the substantial ramparts of the Iron Age hill fort and thus provided an ideal location to breed rabbits. The presence of [[pillow mounds]] and vermin traps demonstrate management of the site for husbandry.{{sfn|Atthill|1976|p = 92}} [[Ridge and furrow]] agriculture has also been identified, from aerial photographs, within the fort.<ref>{{PastScape|mnumber=1494886|access-date=24 August 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> Some of these structures, along with earlier Iron Age features, have been damaged by subsequent quarrying which may have been for [[lead]], [[ochre]] or [[Calamine (mineral)|calamine]].{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 17}}<ref>{{PastScape|mnumber=1494887|access-date=24 August 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The site was described by [[John Leland (antiquary)|John Leland]] in the 16th century.{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 4}} A three-storey building, believed to be the warrener's house and possibly a watch tower, surrounded by a garden, was in ruins by 1830.{{sfn|Bowden|2009|pp = 7–11}}<ref>{{PastScape|mnumber=1494857|access-date=24 August 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>
[[File:Dolebury Warren.jpg|thumb|Dolebury Warren 30 minutes after sunrise looking east by northeast showing the northern, eastern, and southern ramparts. Photograph taken January 2024.]]

===19th and 20th centuries===

The site was visited in the early 19th century by [[John Skinner (archaeologist)|John Skinner]] and surveyed in 1872 by [[Charles William Dymond]].{{sfn|Bowden|2009|p = 3}} In 1906 the Mendip Lodge Estate, which included Dolebury Warren, was sold.<ref>{{cite news|title=Sale of Mendip Lodge|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000265/19060914/121/0016|access-date=23 August 2014|work=Western Times|date=14 September 1906| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It was first scheduled as an [[ancient monument]] in 1929.<ref name="nhle">{{NHLE|desc=Dolebury Camp: a large univallate hillfort and associated and later earthworks on Dolebury Warren|num=1008184|access-date=23 August 2014|fewer-links=yes}}</ref><ref>{{PastScape|mname=Dolebury Camp|mnumber=194279|access-date=16 March 2011|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> In 1935 Dolebury Camp was bought by Miss V. Wills of the [[W.D. & H.O. Wills]] tobacco company to prevent development.<ref>{{cite news|title=Dolbury Camp Saved|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000515/19350824/146/0015|access-date=23 August 2014|work=Bath Chronicle and Weekly Gazette|date=24 August 1935| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Dolebury Warren was notified as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in 1952.<ref name="sssisheet" /> The freehold of {{convert|92.657|ha}} was acquired by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1983 from A. G. Gosling, D. F. Gosling and J. M. Kent, and is managed by the [[Avon Wildlife Trust]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Acquisitions Up to December 2011 |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheader=application%2Fpdf&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=MDT-Type&blobheadername3=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B+filename%3D297%252F965%252Fnt_acquisitions_dec2011-2%252C2.pdf&blobheadervalue2=abinary%3B+charset%3DUTF-8&blobheadervalue3=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1349117284549&ssbinary=true |publisher=National Trust |access-date=24 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714144751/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/cs/Satellite?blobcol=urldata&blobheader=application%2Fpdf&blobheadername1=Content-Disposition&blobheadername2=MDT-Type&blobheadername3=Content-Type&blobheadervalue1=inline%3B%2Bfilename%3D297%2F965%2Fnt_acquisitions_dec2011-2%2C2.pdf&blobheadervalue2=abinary%3B%2Bcharset%3DUTF-8&blobheadervalue3=application%2Fpdf&blobkey=id&blobtable=MungoBlobs&blobwhere=1349117284549&ssbinary=true |archive-date=14 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Mendip Hills. Things to see and do|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/mendip-hills/things-to-see-and-do/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=24 August 2014}}</ref>

==Ecology==

The site of the fort and warren is now grassy slopes which attract a wide range of wild flowers and butterflies.<ref name=awt>{{cite web|title=Dolebury Warren|url=http://www.avonwildlifetrust.org.uk/reserves/dolebury-warren|publisher=Avon Wildlife Trust|access-date=23 August 2014}}</ref> The differing soil types provide suitable habitats for both [[calcifuge|acid-]] and [[calcicole|lime-loving]] plants.{{sfn|Atthill|1976|p=42}} [[Anthyllis vulneraria|Kidney vetch]] (''Anthyllis vulneraria''), [[Campanula rotundifolia|harebell]] (''Campanula rotundifolia'') and [[Cirsium eriophorum|woolly thistle]] (''Cirsium eriophorum'') thrive on the dry stony soils. [[Galium saxatile|Heath bedstraw]] (''Galium saxatile'') and [[Teucrium scorodonia|wood sage]] (''Teucrium scorodonia'') are found in more acidic areas. The higher areas support [[Erica cinerea|bell heather]] (''Erica cinerea''), [[Ulex gallii|western gorse]] (''Ulex gallii'') and [[Calluna vulgaris|common heather]] (''Calluna vulgaris''). Trees and shrubs include the [[Viburnum lantana|wayfaring tree]] (''Viburnum lantana''), [[Viburnum opulus|guelder rose]] (''Viburnum opulus''), [[Sorbus aria|whitebeam]] (''Sorbus aria''), [[Ligustrum vulgare|privet]] (''Ligustrum vulgare'') and [[Cornus sanguinea|dogwood]] (''Cornus sanguinea'').<ref name=sssisheet>{{cite web|title=SSSI citation sheet for Dolebury Warren |url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1002660.pdf |publisher=English Nature |access-date=23 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303185158/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1002660.pdf |archive-date=3 March 2016}}</ref>

Scarce plants found at the warren include [[Sagina nodosa|knotted pearlwort]] (''Sagina nodosa''),{{sfn|Myles|2000|p=81}} and [[Galium pumilum|slender bedstraw]] (''Galium pumilum'').{{sfn|Myles|2000|p=191}} Butterflies recorded here include the [[small blue]] (''Cupido minimus''), [[Melanargia galathea|marbled white]] (''Melanargia galathea''), [[dingy skipper]] (''Erynnis tages''), [[grizzled skipper]] (''Pyrgus malvae''), [[small pearl-bordered fritillary]] (''Boloria selene''), and [[wall brown]] (''Lasiommata megera'').<ref name=awt/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ukbutterflies.co.uk/sites_square.php?square=ST&species=All|title=Sites for National Grid Square: ST|website=UK Butterflies|access-date=24 August 2014}}</ref>

6000732.extract:
Crook Peak to Shute Shelve Hill is a 332.2 hectare (820.9 acre) geological and biological Site of Special Scientific Interest near the western end of the Mendip Hills, Somerset. The line of hills runs for approximately 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) from west to east and includes: Crook Peak, Compton Hill, Wavering Down, Cross Plain and Shute Shelve Hill. Most of the site is owned by the National Trust, which bought 725 acres (293 ha) in 1985, and much of it has been designated as common land. It was notified as an SSSI by Natural England in 1952.
The ecology of the area includes ancient woodland and calcareous grassland which supports nationally rare species including the Cheddar pink. The underlying rocks are Carboniferous Limestone containing phreatic caves at Shute Shelve Cavern and Picken's Hole from which fossils dating from the Middle Devensian have been recovered.
