'''Crook Peak to Shute Shelve Hill''' is a 332.2 [[hectare]] (820.9 acre) [[Geological Site of Special Scientific Interest|geological]] and [[biological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] near the western end of the [[Mendip Hills]], [[Somerset]]. The line of hills runs for approximately {{convert|5|km}} from west to east and includes: '''Crook Peak''', '''Compton Hill''', '''Wavering Down''', '''Cross Plain''' and '''Shute Shelve Hill'''. Most of the site is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]], which bought {{convert|725|acre}} in 1985,<ref>{{cite news|title=Trust fundraising push reached new heights|url=http://www.westerndailypress.co.uk/Trust-fundraising-push-reached-new-heights/story-12334854-detail/story.html|access-date=26 April 2015|work=Western Daily Press|date=9 September 2010|archive-url=https://archive.today/20150426124654/http://www.westerndailypress.co.uk/Trust-fundraising-push-reached-new-heights/story-12334854-detail/story.html|archive-date=26 April 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref> and much of it has been designated as [[common land]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Crooks Peak and Compton Bishop Hill|url=http://common-land.com/lands/view/2468|publisher=Common Land in England|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> It was [[SSSI notification|notified]] as an SSSI by [[Natural England]] in 1952.

The ecology of the area includes [[ancient woodland]] and [[calcareous grassland]] which supports nationally rare species including the [[Dianthus gratianopolitanus|Cheddar pink]]. The underlying rocks are [[Carboniferous Limestone]] containing [[phreatic]] caves at [[Shute Shelve Cavern]] and [[Picken's Hole]] from which fossils dating from the [[Last glacial period|Middle Devensian]] have been recovered.

== Description ==

The site extends for some {{convert|5|km}} from west to east. Near its eastern end it is divided by a gap used by the [[A38 road]] and the disused [[Cheddar Valley Line|Cheddar Valley railway line]]. At the western end of the hills, closest to the [[M5 motorway]], is Crook Peak which reaches {{convert|191|m|ft}}, and forms a prominent feature from the surrounding landscape.<ref>{{cite web|title=Crook Peak|url=http://www.goodrunguide.co.uk/RecommendedRoutes/2641|publisher=Good run guide|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Crook Peak|url=http://www.ukclimbing.com/logbook/crag.php?id=17490|publisher=UK Climbing|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> Evidence of early human occupation of Crook Peak includes a polished [[flint]] [[axe]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Winscombe Parish — A more detailed history. Early Settlement |url=http://www.winscombeandsandfordpc.org.uk/wpchistory.php |publisher=Winscombe and Sandford Parish Council |access-date=26 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524110751/http://www.winscombeandsandfordpc.org.uk/wpchistory.php |archive-date=24 May 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It was used as the site of a beacon at the time of the [[Spanish Armada]].<ref name=countryfile>{{cite web|last1=Dommett|first1=Pete|title=Crook Peak, Mendip Hills|url=http://www.countryfile.com/days-out/crook-peak-mendip-hills|website=Countryfile|publisher=BBC|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref>  A ridge to the south east of Crook Peak, known as 'The Razor', is used by the [[West Mendip Soaring Association]] to fly [[model aircraft]] when the wind is a south-westerly, southerly or north-easterly direction.<ref>{{cite web|title=Our location|url=http://www.westmendipsoaring.org.uk/index.php/club-information/find-us|publisher=West Mendip Soaring Association|access-date=21 April 2015}}</ref>
[[File:WaveringDown2.jpg|thumb|View of Wavering Down from Cross Plain.]]
Compton Hill is above the village of [[Compton Bishop]]. Also within the parish of Compton Bishop is Wavering Down which reaches a height of {{convert|210|m|ft}},<ref>{{cite book|last1=Roberts|first1=James|title=Walking in Somerset|date=1997|publisher=Cicerone Press|isbn=978-1-85284-253-6|pages=102–106|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IhLY0WZUtRsC&q=Compton+Hill+Somerset+Crook+Peak&pg=PA102}}</ref> and is marked with a [[triangulation station]].<ref>{{cite web|title=TP6778 - Wavering Down|url=http://trigpointing.uk/trig/6778|publisher=Trig Pointing UK|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> Around the small village of [[Cross, Somerset|Cross]] is Wavering Down House which was, for the last 20 years of his life, the home of the British comedian [[Frankie Howerd]].<ref name = "BBC 17m2006">{{cite web|url =http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/programmes/newsnight/4813788.stm|first = Stephen|last = Smith|publisher = [[BBC]] |date = 17 March 2007|title = Titter ye not — it's Frankie's pad|access-date= 16 October 2007}}</ref> The house is now a [[tourist attraction]], and in the summer hosts concerts and opens regularly as a museum of Howerd's collection of [[memorabilia]] to raise fund for charities.<ref name = "BBC 17m2006"/> Above the village itself is Cross Plain where there are [[Earthworks (archaeology)|earthworks]] remaining from [[Enclosure (archaeology)|enclosures]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Enclosures, Kings Wood, Compton Bishop|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/11482|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> Further east is Shute Shelve Hill, east of the A38 road, reaching a height of {{convert|233|m|ft}}, above the town of [[Axbridge]] and adjoining [[Axbridge Hill and Fry's Hill]].

A long-distance footpath, the [[Mendip Way]], follows much of the northern boundary of the site. There is also a {{convert|165|m}} long tunnel which was part of the [[Cheddar Valley Line]] but is now used by pedestrians and cyclists.<ref>{{cite web|title=Exploring the Strawberry Line|url=http://www.thestrawberryline.org.uk/index.php?section=visit|publisher=Strawberry Line|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> Within the tunnel the central surface has been paved with tarmac, but it is unlit except for a central guide line of small guide lamps. The north half of the tunnel is brick lined, but about midway it reverts to unlined rock for the southern half, marking a change in the underlying geology from sandstone to limestone.<ref>{{cite web|title=Exploring the Strawberry Line|url=http://www.thestrawberryline.org.uk/index.php?section=visit|publisher=The Strawberry Line|access-date=22 April 2015}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
Crook Peak has been important as a landmark and boundary from very early times, and the origins of the name are unclear. The local parish council state that 'Crook' comes from the [[Old English]] 'Cruc' meaning 'peak' or 'pointed hill'.<ref>{{cite web | title=Winscombe Parish | url=http://www.winscombeandsandfordpc.org.uk/wpchistory.php | access-date=7 October 2010 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150524110751/http://www.winscombeandsandfordpc.org.uk/wpchistory.php | archive-date=24 May 2015 | url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=Not a soul in the West Mendips | work=Times Online | url=http://travel.timesonline.co.uk/article/0,,20489-2100264,00.html | access-date=18 July 2006 | location=London | date=25 March 2006}}{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> 'Shute' is a contraction of ''schute'' which meant slope in the [[Middle Ages]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Costen|first1=Michael D.|last2=Aston|first2=Mick A.|title=An early medieval secular and ecclesiastical estate: the origins of the parish of Winscombe, North Somerset.|journal=Somerset Archaeology and Natural History|date=2008|volume=151|pages=139–158|url=http://www.sanhs.org/Documents/151/AstonCosten.pdf|access-date=26 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170819062351/http://www.sanhs.org/Documents/151/AstonCosten.pdf|archive-date=19 August 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Biological ==
[[File:KingsWoodSomerset.jpg|thumb|King's Wood between Cross Plain and Shute Shelve Hill]]
The ecology of the site is varied. There are ancient and secondary semi-natural [[Ancient woodland|broadleaved woodland]]; however, the majority is unimproved [[calcareous grassland]] with calcareous grassland and [[acidic]] dry dwarf-shrub heath.<ref>{{cite web|title=Landscape Assessment of the Mendip Hills|url=http://www.mendip.gov.uk/CHttpHandler.ashx?id=1882&p=0|publisher=Mendip AONB|access-date=22 April 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304111450/http://www.mendip.gov.uk/CHttpHandler.ashx?id=1882&p=0|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> Four of the calcareous
grassland communities and two of the woodland types have a restricted distribution in Britain, as does the calcareous grassland/acidic dry dwarf-shrub heath. These support species, four of which are considered nationally rare, while seven of the plant species present are considered notable. Plants of interest include the nationally rare [[Cheddar pink]] (''Dianthus gratianopolitanus''), [[bedstraw]] (''Galium fleurotii''), [[Carex humilis|dwarf sedge]] (''Carex humilis'') and [[dwarf mouse-ear]] (''Cerastium pumilum''). Rose Wood and King's Wood are ancient woodland sites. King's Wood has [[Coppicing|coppiced]] [[hazel]] and nationally important [[Tilia cordata|small leaved lime]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Village Design Statement The Parish of Compton Bishop|url=http://s3.spanglefish.com/s/2829/documents/village%20design%20statement/vdsapril2003v12.pdf|publisher=Compton Bishop|access-date=26 April 2015|page=3}}</ref> The nationally rare [[Lithospermum purpurocaeruleum|purple gromwell]] (''Lithospermum purpurocaeruleum'') occurs at Rose Wood.<ref name="englishnature">{{cite web|title=Crook Peak to Shute Shelve Hill |work=English Nature |url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001580.pdf |access-date=17 July 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061013121343/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001580.pdf |archive-date=13 October 2006 |df=dmy }}</ref>

== Geological ==
Shute Shelve Hill, is largely formed by more resistant [[Carboniferous Limestone]] laid down in the [[Dinantian]] period about 350 million years ago. The hill rises to {{convert|233|m}} above sea levels and represents a ridge formed by the southern Limb of a highly eroded [[anticline]] with younger limestones on the lower slopes.<ref>{{cite book|last=Haslett|first=Simon K.|title=Somerset Landscapes: Geology and landforms|year=2010|publisher=Blackbarn Books|location=Usk|isbn=978-1-4564-1631-7|pages=38–41}}</ref> [[Black Rock Limestone]] is exposed at several sites but is commonly covered by [[Burrington Oolite]].<ref name=bgs>{{cite web|title=Crook Peak and Axbridge|url=https://www.bgs.ac.uk/mendips/localities/crookpeak.html|publisher=British Geological Survey|access-date=22 April 2015}}</ref>

[[Picken's Hole]] at the southern end of Crook Peak is considered to be of importance because of its clear, well-stratified sequence of deposits and faunas, all dating from within the [[Wisconsin glaciation|Devensian]]. The cave is {{convert|8|m}} below the plateau and {{convert|27|m}} above the valley floor.<ref>{{cite web|title=Picken's Hole (Scragg's Hole), near White Rock, Compton Bishop|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/10459|website=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=26 April 2015}}</ref> It is named after M.J. Picken who found teeth in earth thrown out of their sets in the area by badgers.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Tratman|first1=E.K.|title=Picken's Hole, Crook Peak, Somerset: A Pleistocene Site|journal=Proceedings of the University of Bristol Spelaeological Society|date=1964|volume=10|issue=2|pages=112–115|url=http://www.ubss.org.uk/resources/proceedings/vol10/UBSS_Proc_10_2_112-115.pdf}}</ref> A large number of [[Middle Palaeolithic]] artefacts, and two [[Neanderthal]] teeth dated to about 55,000 years [[Before Present|BP]], have been recovered from the cave.<ref name=nhle>{{cite web|title=Picken's Hole |url=https://www.historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1010715 |website=National Heritage List for England |publisher=Historic England }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The British Palaeolithic: Human Societies at the Edge of the Pleistocene World|first1=Paul|last1=Pettitt|first2=Mark|last2=White|publisher=Routledge|year=2012|pages=364–65|location=Abingdon, UK|isbn=978-0-415-67455-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Smith|first=David Ingle|title=Limestone and Caves of the Mendip Hills|year=1975|publisher=[[David & Charles]]|isbn=978-0-7153-6572-4|pages=360–361}}</ref> Faunal deposits of [[spotted hyena]], [[lion]], [[Arctic fox]], [[mammoth]], [[woolly rhinoceros]], [[horse]], [[reindeer]], [[European ground squirrel|suslik]] and northern vole (''[[Microtus oeconomus]]'') from approximately 35,000 [[Before Present|BP]] have also been recovered.<ref>{{cite web|title=Crook Peak to Shute Shelve Hill SSSI citation sheet |url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001580.pdf |publisher=English Nature |access-date=26 April 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303201751/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1001580.pdf |archive-date=3 March 2016 |df=dmy }}</ref>

[[Shute Shelve Cavern]] is located on Shute Shelve Hill. It is a natural cave system which was mined for its [[yellow ochre]], until the 1920s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bgs.ac.uk/mendips/localities/crookpeak.html|title=Crook Peak and Axbridge|publisher=[[British Geological Survey]]|access-date=7 July 2009}}</ref> The [[phreatic]] cave contains fossils of [[speleothems]] over 350,000 years old.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Farrant|first1=A.R.|last2=Gray|first2=A.|title=Shute Shelve Cavern. Exploration, History and Geomorphology|journal=Proceedings of the University of Bristol Spelaeology Society|date=1993|volume=3|pages=283–290|url=http://www.ubss.org.uk/resources/proceedings/vol19/UBSS_Proc_19_3_283-290.pdf}}</ref>

== Barton Camp ==
Barton Camp, which is on the northern slopes of Crook Peak, is run by the Bristol Children's Help Society, which was founded in 1884 to help needy children. The centre provided residential activity courses. The facilities include classrooms, a sports hall, outdoor pool, playing field and bunkhouse accommodation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Barton Camp|url=http://www.bartoncamp.co.uk/|publisher=The Bristol Children's Help Society|access-date=21 April 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | author = Steve Eggington |date=August 2006 | title = '''Serious Playtime''' | journal = Mendip Times | volume = 2 | issue = 3 | pages = 10–11 | url = http://www.mendiptimes.co.uk/ }}</ref>

6032371.title: Coleridge Cottage
6032371.extract:
Coleridge Cottage is a cottage situated in Nether Stowey, Bridgwater, Somerset, England. It is a grade II* listed building. The 17th century cottage was originally two buildings which were later combined and expanded.
In 1797 the poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge rented the cottage. While he lived there he wrote many of his better known works. He was visited by William Wordsworth and other early members of the Romantic movement. Coleridge moved out in 1799 and the building was refurbished. Almost 100 years after his occupation some of his admirers leased the property and eventually bought it, after a national campaign and significant private funding. In 1909 they handed it over to the National Trust who have run it as a writer's home museum since then. In the later 20th and early 21st centuries further renovation and expansion was undertaken. Since then, it has won awards as a tourist attraction.
The cottage is the starting point for the long-distance trail the Coleridge Way which runs west for 51 miles (82 km) to Lynmouth.

35, Lime Street, [[Nether Stowey]] |image_size = 200 |map_type = Somerset |map_caption = Location within [[Somerset]] and the United Kingdom |coordinates = {{coord|51.1522|-3.1579|display=inline,title}} |established = 1998 |location = [[Nether Stowey]], [[Somerset]] |type = |visitors = |director = |curator = |public_transit= |website = [http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/coleridge-cottage/ Coleridge Cottage information at the National Trust] }} '''Coleridge Cottage''' is a [[cottage]] situated in [[Nether Stowey]], [[Bridgwater]], [[Somerset]], England. It is a grade II* [[listed building]].{{NHLE|num=1344921|desc=Coleridge's Cottage|access-date=6 June 2022}} The 17th century cottage was originally two buildings which were later combined and expanded. In 1797 the poet [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] rented the cottage. While he lived there he wrote many of his better known works. He was visited by [[William Wordsworth]] and other early members of the [[Romanticism|Romantic movement]]. Coleridge moved out in 1799 and the building was refurbished. Almost 100 years after his occupation some of his admirers leased the property and eventually bought it, after a national campaign and significant private funding. In 1909 they handed it over to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] who have run it as a [[writer's home museum]] since then. In the later 20th and early 21st centuries further renovation and expansion was undertaken. Since then, it has won awards as a tourist attraction. The cottage is the starting point for the [[long-distance trail]] the [[Coleridge Way]] which runs west for 51 miles (82 km) to [[Lynmouth]].{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Long Distance Walkers Association Coleridge Way |url=https://www.ldwa.org.uk/ |access-date=2022-06-10 |website=www.ldwa.org.uk |language=en-GB}} ==History== [[File:Cottage Moore.jpg|thumb|left|The cottage when it was 'Moore's Coleridge Cottage Inn', around 1890]] The cottage was constructed in the 17th century as two attached buildings. One contained a parlour, kitchen and service room on the ground floor and three corresponding bed chambers above,{{cite web |url=http://www.friendsofcoleridge.com/national-trust-website |title=Coleridge Cottage |access-date=6 February 2015 |publisher=Friends of Coleridge |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224101624/http://www.friendsofcoleridge.com/national-trust-website |archive-date=24 December 2013 |url-status=dead }} and an adjoining byre or barn. The poet [[Samuel Taylor Coleridge]] rented the cottage for three years from 1797. As well as writing poetry he was a literary critic and philosopher who, with his friend [[William Wordsworth]], was a founder of the [[Romanticism|Romantic Movement]] in England and a member of the [[Lake Poets]]. It was while he was living in [[Nether Stowey]] that Coleridge wrote ''[[This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison]]'', ''[[The Rime of the Ancient Mariner]]'', part of ''[[Christabel (poem)|Christabel]]'', and ''[[Frost at Midnight]]''.{{cite web |url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/somerset/content/articles/2005/03/17/the_coleridge_way_walk_feature.shtml |title=Walk The Coleridge Way |access-date=12 February 2008 |work=BBC Somerset }} While writing ''[[Kubla Khan|Kubla Khan; or, A Vision in a Dream: A Fragment]]'', Coleridge was said to have been interrupted by the arrival of "a [[person on business from Porlock]]". It is unclear whether this really happened or was part of a dream but has become a literary allusion for unwanted intruders who disrupt inspired creativity.{{cite news|last1=Osborne|first1=Victor|title=Literary landscape: Coleridge's Somerset|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3302297/Literary-landscape-Coleridges-Somerset.html|access-date=6 February 2015|work=Telegraph|date=6 July 2002}} During Coleridge's time at the house [[William Wordsworth]] visited him and subsequently rented [[Alfoxton House|Alfoxton Park]], a little over {{convert|3|mi}} away.{{cite web|last1=Baggs|first1=A.P.|last2=Siraut|first2=M. C.|title=Stringston|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/som/vol6/pp170-172|website=British History Online|publisher=Victoria County History|access-date=6 February 2015}} There are references to the cottage in several of Coleridge's poems, including ''To The Rev G Coleridge'' (lines 52–61), ''This Lime Tree Bower My Prison''; ''Frost at Midnight''; and ''Fears in Solitude'' (lines 221–226). The cottage was refurbished in 1800 and run as an inn. Further major work took place in the second half of the 19th century when rooms were added at the back of the building and the roof was raised. In 1893 a committee of Coleridge's admirers took a lease on the property for 15 years at £15 per annum, however by 1896 an appeal had been launched to try to raise more money for the lease or eventual purchase,{{cite news|title=Coleridge's Cottage|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000330/18960501/081/0007|work=Dover Express|date=1 May 1896| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }} with the threat that it could be removed to America.{{cite news|title=The Purchase of Coleridge's Cottage|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000344/19080627/071/0010|access-date=16 July 2014|work=Morpeth Herald|date=27 June 1908| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }} They installed the commemorative plaque on the wall which was unveiled on 9 June 1893. By 1908 the campaign, chaired by the [[Earl of Lytton]], had gained public support including that of the archbishops of [[Archbishop of Canterbury|Canterbury]] and [[Archbishop of York|York]], and raised the funds needed to purchase the property.{{cite news|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000576/19071002/091/0006|title=Coleridge's Cottage|work=Aberdeen Journal|date=2 October 1907| publisher = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription |access-date=16 July 2014}} ==National Trust ownership== [[File:Commemorative plaque - geograph.org.uk - 1766822.jpg|thumb|Commemorative plaque installed in 1893.]] Having served for many years as 'Moore's Coleridge Cottage Inn', the building was acquired for the nation in 1908, and the following year it was handed over to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]].{{cite journal|last1=Miall|first1=David S.|title=The Campaign to Acquire Coleridge Cottage|journal=The Wordsworth Circle|date=1991|volume=22|issue=1|pages=82–88|url=https://www.ualberta.ca/~dmiall/Essays/ColeridgeCottage.htm|access-date=9 March 2015}} On 23 May 1998, following a £25,000 appeal by the Friends of Coleridge and the National Trust, two further rooms on the first floor were officially opened by [[William Coleridge, 5th Baron Coleridge|Lord Coleridge]] a descendant of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. In 2011 the National Trust undertook a major re-presentation project that also saw the opening of additional rooms. The oldest parts of the cottage are now presented as the Coleridge family might have known them, with the original [[inglenook]] fireplace in the parlour uncovered and working once more.{{cite news|last1=Morris|first1=Steven|title=Samuel Taylor Coleridge's cottage to reopen after revamp|url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2011/sep/09/samuel-taylor-coleridge-fireplace-cottage-revamp|access-date=6 February 2015|work=Guardian|date=9 September 2011}} The garden was opened to visitors for the first time, complete with an 18th-century vegetable plot, a wildflower area and representations of Coleridge's animals.{{cite web|title=Coleridge Cottage|url=http://www.somersetroutes.co.uk/userfiles/downloads/14/Coleridge%20Cottage%20Welcome%20Leaflet.pdf|format=PDF|publisher=Somerset Routes|access-date=2 July 2014|archive-date=14 July listen to poetry at audio posts around the garden and the well is operational once more and can be seen in the small courtyard behind the cottage.{{cite web|title=Coleridge Cottage
